title: “The words of the Preacher, the son of David, king in Jerusalem” — who is the Preacher?
summary: Ecclesiastes 1:1 gives the speaker as “the Preacher, the son of David, king in Jerusalem”, and 1:12 as the Preacher who “was king over Israel in Jerusalem”. The verses quoted do not name him.
text: KJV Ecclesiastes 1:1: “The words of the Preacher, the son of David, king in Jerusalem.” KJV Ecclesiastes 1:12: “I the Preacher was king over Israel in Jerusalem.” KJV Ecclesiastes 1:16: “I communed with mine own heart, saying, Lo, I am come to great estate, and have gotten more wisdom than all they that have been before me in Jerusalem: yea, my heart had great experience of wisdom and knowledge.” KJV Ecclesiastes 2:7–9: “I got me servants and maidens, and had servants born in my house; also I had great possessions of great and small cattle above all that were in Jerusalem before me:” “I gathered me also silver and gold, and the peculiar treasure of kings and of the provinces: I gat me men singers and women singers, and the delights of the sons of men, as musical instruments, and that of all sorts.” “So I was great, and increased more than all that were before me in Jerusalem: also my wisdom remained with me.” KJV Ecclesiastes 12:9: “And moreover, because the preacher was wise, he still taught the people knowledge; yea, he gave good heed, and sought out, and set in order many proverbs.” A search of the packaged KJV text of Ecclesiastes for the word “Solomon” finds nothing.
reasoning: The book gives the speaker a title, “the Preacher”, and three descriptions: a son of David, a king in Jerusalem, and one who “was king over Israel in Jerusalem”. In 1:16 and 2:7–9 he says he surpassed “all they that have been before me in Jerusalem”. The verses quoted do not give a personal name. Possible readings: a son of David who reigned in Jerusalem, so that the descriptions point to one king; another son or descendant of David who reigned there; or a speaking voice that the book frames by a title and a description of a king without the framing being a claim about one historical person. The record does not decide between them.
scope: Q marks a question the passage leaves open. It is not a finding of contradiction or of scientific error. The question is limited to the verses quoted; the word search covers the packaged KJV text of Ecclesiastes only and is a word search. The record does not say that any reading is the right one, and does not rest on the Hebrew or the Greek.

title: “Which are given from one shepherd” — who is the one shepherd in Ecclesiastes 12:11?
summary: Ecclesiastes 12:11 says the words of the wise “are given from one shepherd”. The verses quoted do not say who the shepherd is.
text: KJV Ecclesiastes 12:9–11: “And moreover, because the preacher was wise, he still taught the people knowledge; yea, he gave good heed, and sought out, and set in order many proverbs.” “The preacher sought to find out acceptable words: and that which was written was upright, even words of truth.” “The words of the wise are as goads, and as nails fastened by the masters of assemblies, which are given from one shepherd.” KJV Ecclesiastes 12:12–13: “And further, by these, my son, be admonished: of making many books there is no end; and much study is a weariness of the flesh.” “Let us hear the conclusion of the whole matter: Fear God, and keep his commandments: for this is the whole duty of man.” A search of the packaged KJV text of Ecclesiastes for “shepherd” finds 12:11 only.
reasoning: Verse 9 speaks of the preacher who taught the people knowledge, verse 10 of what he sought and wrote, and verse 11 says the words of the wise “are given from one shepherd”. The verse does not say who the shepherd is, or whether the words given are the preacher’s own, a collection of sayings of several wise men, or the book’s teaching as a whole. Possible readings: the Lord, as the source of the words; the preacher of verses 9–10, as the one who gave them to the people; or a human teacher or leader whom the verse does not name. The record does not decide between them.

title: “The king hath brought me into his chambers” — is the speaker’s beloved the king and Solomon?
summary: The Song of Solomon has the woman speak of “my beloved” and also of “the king” and of “king Solomon”. The verses quoted do not say in terms whether “my beloved” and the king are the same person.
text: KJV Song of Solomon 1:1: “The song of songs, which is Solomon's.” KJV Song of Solomon 1:4: “Draw me, we will run after thee: the king hath brought me into his chambers: we will be glad and rejoice in thee, we will remember thy love more than wine: the upright love thee.” KJV Song of Solomon 1:7: “Tell me, O thou whom my soul loveth, where thou feedest, where thou makest thy flock to rest at noon: for why should I be as one that turneth aside by the flocks of thy companions?” KJV Song of Solomon 1:12: “While the king sitteth at his table, my spikenard sendeth forth the smell thereof.” KJV Song of Solomon 2:16: “My beloved is mine, and I am his: he feedeth among the lilies.” KJV Song of Solomon 3:7: “Behold his bed, which is Solomon's; threescore valiant men are about it, of the valiant of Israel.” KJV Song of Solomon 3:11: “Go forth, O ye daughters of Zion, and behold king Solomon with the crown wherewith his mother crowned him in the day of his espousals, and in the day of the gladness of his heart.” KJV Song of Solomon 8:12: “My vineyard, which is mine, is before me: thou, O Solomon, must have a thousand, and those that keep the fruit thereof two hundred.”
reasoning: The woman calls the one she loves “my beloved” (2:16) and “thou whom my soul loveth” (1:7), and in 1:7 she asks where he feeds his flock; in 2:16 “he feedeth among the lilies”. She also speaks of “the king” who “hath brought me into his chambers” (1:4) and “sitteth at his table” (1:12), and the daughters of Zion are told to “behold king Solomon” on the day of his espousals (3:11). In 8:12 someone is addressed as “O Solomon”, and the verses quoted do not say whether that is her beloved. Possible readings: the beloved and the king are one person, the king Solomon of 3:11; the beloved is a shepherd and the king is a different person whom she speaks of; or “king” and “Solomon” are names of address for the beloved that the verses quoted do not equate with him. The record does not decide between them.
